n: Advice for dining with a powerful person: be careful and pay attention to what (or who) is in front of you.

f.w: consider diligently what is before thee
f.g: Or “who is before you”—be aware of the ruler’s motives.

n: A vivid way to say “control your appetite”: put a knife to your throat if you tend to overindulge.

f.g: Greedy, inclined to overeat.

n: Don’t crave the ruler’s delicacies, because that food may be a trap—offered to win influence over you.

f.g: dainties = delicacies, fancy food.

n: Don’t wear yourself out to get rich; have the good sense to stop.
Riches vanish in a blink—they sprout wings and fly off like an eagle. Strikingly, an Egyptian wisdom text uses a similar image of riches flying away like geese.
Don’t eat with a stingy person or crave his fancy food.

f.g: A stingy, grudging attitude (the opposite of the “bountiful eye” of 22:9).

n: He’s always counting the cost. He says “eat and drink,” but he doesn’t mean it. A person’s true character is what is in his heart.

f.w: as he thinketh in his heart, so is he
f.g: In context: he is the kind of man who calculates in his heart.

n: You’ll regret the bite you ate and waste your polite compliments on him.

f.g: Your pleasant words will have been wasted.

n: Don’t waste wise words on fools; they’ll only scorn them.

f.w: Speak not in the ears of a fool

n: Don’t move old boundary stones or steal the fields of orphans.

f.g: Orphans, among the most vulnerable in ancient society.

n: Their Redeemer is strong and will take up their case against you. A “redeemer” (go’el) was a close relative who defended family rights; here God himself is the defender. Latter-day Saints see in this title the Redeemer, Jesus Christ.

f.g: Hebrew go’el—a kinsman-protector who rescued family members and land.

n: Commit your heart to discipline and your ears to knowledge.
Don’t hold back correction from a child; discipline won’t kill him. The ancient world used physical punishment; the lasting principle is that loving correction protects a child.

f.w: Withhold not correction from the child

n: Correction can save a child from ruin and early death. The parent’s goal is the child’s life, not punishment for its own sake.

f.g: Hebrew Sheol—the grave, death.

n: A parent speaks with emotion: if your heart is wise, my heart will be glad too.
My innermost being will rejoice when you speak what is right.

f.g: reins = kidneys; in Hebrew thought, the seat of the deepest emotions.

n: Don’t envy sinners; keep reverencing the Lord all day long.

f.w: Let not thine heart envy sinners

n: There truly is a future, and your hope will not be cut off. The righteous can trust that things will be set right.

f.w: thine expectation shall not be cut off

n: Listen, my child, be wise, and keep your heart on the right path.

f.w: guide thine heart in the way

n: Don’t join heavy drinkers or those who gorge on meat.

f.g: winebibbers = heavy drinkers.
Gluttons who gorge themselves on meat.

n: Drunkards and gluttons end up poor, and their drowsiness leaves them in rags.

f.w: drowsiness shall clothe a man with rags

n: Listen to the father who gave you life, and don’t look down on your mother when she is old. Honoring parents continues through their old age.

f.w: despise not thy mother when she is old

n: Buy truth and never sell it—along with wisdom, instruction, and understanding. Truth is worth any price and shouldn’t be traded away.

f.w: Buy the truth, and sell it not

n: The father of a righteous child greatly rejoices; a wise child brings joy.
Let your father and mother be glad—give her who bore you reason to rejoice.

f.g: Your mother, who gave birth to you.

n: The father pleads, “Give me your heart,” and watch my example. Real teaching is about trust and example, not just rules.
A prostitute is like a deep ditch, and an adulteress a narrow well—easy to fall into, hard to escape.

f.g: A narrow well shaft—once in, hard to climb out.

n: She lies in wait like a robber and multiplies the unfaithful among men.

f.w: lieth in wait as for a prey

n: A series of questions builds a portrait: who has misery, fights, complaints, unexplained bruises, and bloodshot eyes?

f.g: Bloodshot or dull eyes from drinking.
Complaining, endless talk.

n: The answer: those who linger over wine and keep going after mixed drinks.

f.g: Wine mixed with spices to make it stronger.
tarry = linger, stay long.

n: Don’t gaze at wine when it sparkles red in the cup and goes down smoothly. Temptation often starts with looking.

f.g: When it goes down smoothly.

f.w: Look not thou upon the wine

n: In the end it bites like a snake and poisons like a viper.

f.g: adder = a venomous snake, a viper.

n: Under the influence, your eyes will see strange things and your mind will speak nonsense—or, as some read it, you’ll look at other women.

f.g: Hebrew can mean “strange things” (hallucinations) or “strange women.”

n: The drunk feels like someone lying in the middle of the sea or perched atop a ship’s swaying mast—dizzy and unstable.

f.w: upon the top of a mast
f.g: A picture of the dizzy swaying of drunkenness.

n: The final, sad words of the drunk: “They hit me, but I felt nothing. When will I wake up? I’ll go get another drink.” A vivid picture of addiction.

f.w: I will seek it yet again
